items.canonical_answer: Living standards are the level of material well-being of a person or household: how well they are housed, fed, clothed, schooled and cared for, and how secure that level is. They are usually measured by GDP per head alongside health, education and access indicators.
marking_guidance: Precise definition: the meaning must name material well-being - housing, food, schooling, care - and may add security or the measures used, since a vague answer such as how rich a country is earns nothing.

items.prompt: A country records GDP of N$90 billion in a year, and its population is 3 million people. Calculate GDP per head.
items.canonical_answer: GDP per head = GDP / population. N$90 billion / 3 million people = N$30 000 per person a year.
marking_guidance: The formula - GDP per head = GDP / population - must be stated.
Substitution: the working must show the total divided by the population, using the N$90 billion and 3 million supplied.
The answer with units: N$30 000 per head (per person) a year.

items.prompt: Two districts of Windhoek record the same GDP per head of N$45 000 a year. In Katutura Central, the share of households with piped water is 61%; in the second district, it is 96%. Life expectancy is 57 years in Katutura Central against 71 years in the second district. Explain what these figures show about measuring living standards.
items.canonical_answer: The figures show that health and access indicators can separate two places with the same GDP per head. Both districts record N$45 000, yet piped water reaches 61% of households against 96%, and life expectancy is 57 years against 71. GDP per head is an average that may hide how income is shared and what it buys, while health and access to services are part of living standards in their own right. However, only two indicators are given, and the water gap may partly reflect distance from pipes, not income.
marking_guidance: What the data shows - the relationship must be stated first: equal GDP per head, unequal living-standard indicators.
Supporting evidence - the comparison must be quoted: 61% against 96% on piped water, 57 against 71 years on life expectancy.
The exception or caution earns a mark: however, the indicators shown are not the whole picture.
The why - an explanation of the relationship, through GDP per head as an average that may hide how income is shared - is the core mark; quoting the figures alone is not interpretation.

items.prompt: Oshakati Textiles sponsors a town survey: average GDP per head in Oshakati has risen from N$18 000 to N$30 000 a year over the past decade, yet the share of households with electricity has moved from 55% to just 58%. Using the figures, explain whether average living standards in Oshakati have improved.
items.canonical_answer: GDP per head rose by N$30 000 - N$18 000 = N$12 000 a year, about two-thirds, while electricity access rose by just 3 percentage points, from 55% to 58%. Because GDP per head is an average, the gain may have gone to a minority of households: an average that climbs while a basic service barely moves suggests most homes have not shared in it. So living standards improved on the money measure, provided prices did not rise as fast, but for many households daily life may have changed little.
marking_guidance: Context: the figures - N$18 000 to N$30 000 and 55% to 58% - must anchor the answer, and the extract's town is the setting.
Reasoning: because GDP per head is an average that may hide the sharing, the link from the money figure to household living standards must be given.
Conclusion: therefore the answer must close on the two measures disagreeing and what that means for the town's living standards.

items.canonical_answer: The distribution of income is how a country's total income is shared among its households. It matters for living standards because a household's standard depends not just on the average income the country produces but on where the household sits in that sharing.
marking_guidance: Precise definition: the meaning must name the sharing of total income among households, and may add why it matters for living standards, since a definition of income alone earns partial credit at best.

items.prompt: Namibia and a second economy of equal size both record GDP per head of N$60 000 a year. In Namibia the typical household earns about 40% of that average; in the second economy, about 70%. Analyse how the sharing of income is likely to affect the comparison of living standards between the two economies.
items.canonical_answer: Both economies record GDP per head of N$60 000, but the typical household earns about 0.40 x N$60 000 = N$24 000 a year in Namibia against 0.70 x N$60 000 = N$42 000 in the second economy. Because the typical household's income pays for housing, schooling and healthcare, the living standard it can afford diverges: the Namibian household must cover the same basics from a much smaller income. GDP per head therefore ranks the two equal, while the typical household in the second economy lives materially better; the sharing of income, not the average, decides the comparison. Typical and low-income Namibian households lose most, and the Namibian government faces a greater need for transfers to lift them.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - equal averages of N$60 000 with typical households at 40% and 70% of the average - must be stated.
Mechanism: because the typical household's income pays for the basics, this causes the affordable living standards to diverge.
Consequence: therefore the comparison of living standards must be traced through - the average alone misleads.
For whom: the typical household, low-income households, workers and the government must be named.

items.prompt: Two neighbouring economies of similar population each collect income tax. In the first, a laboratory assistant earning N$60 000 a year pays 12% of it in income tax while a manager earning N$300 000 pays 28%; in the second, both pay a flat 15% of income in tax, and the second economy relies on taxes on basic goods that take about 8% of a low earner's income and 2% of a high earner's. Using the figures, explain what these tax systems suggest about how income and living standards compare between the two economies.
items.canonical_answer: The first economy's income tax is progressive: the high earner pays 28%, the low earner 12%. In the second, the low earner loses 15% + 8% = 23% and the high earner 15% + 2% = 17%, a regressive package. Because households live on take-home income, the first system is likely to narrow the gap between low and high earners and the second to widen it. So low earners in the first economy are likely to live closer to the average, provided pre-tax incomes and prices are similar.
marking_guidance: Context: the figures - the 12% and 28% shares in the first economy, and the 23% against 17% total in the second - must anchor the answer, and the data must be worked.
Reasoning: because take-home income is what a household lives on, the link from each tax system to the sharing of income and to living standards must be given.
Conclusion: therefore the answer must close on what the tax systems mean for the comparison of living standards between the two economies.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. Living standards are best defined as:
A  the total value of goods and services produced in a country
B  the level of material well-being of a person or household
C  the money a government collects in tax
D  the number of people in work

2. GDP per head is calculated as:
A  GDP divided by the population
B  GDP multiplied by the population
C  GDP minus government spending
D  GDP divided by the number of workers

3. A country's GDP is N$40 billion and its population is 2 million. GDP per head is:
A  N$20 000
B  N$80 000
C  N$200 000
D  N$8 000

4. Which indicator captures what GDP per head alone may miss?
A  the total value of output
B  life expectancy and access to clean water
C  the size of the population
D  the exchange rate

5. GDP per head may mislead as a measure of living standards because:
A  it counts farming output and nothing else
B  it is an average that may hide how income is shared
C  it falls whenever the population grows
D  it ignores the price of exports

6. The distribution of income means:
A  how a country's total income is shared among households
B  how GDP is divided between government departments
C  the average income per person
D  the tax a household pays each year

7. Two countries record the same GDP per head. The typical household lives better in the country where:
A  the population is larger
B  income is spread more evenly
C  the exchange rate is higher
D  tax rates are flat

8. An income tax is progressive when:
A  high earners pay a larger share of their income than low earners
B  low earners pay a larger share of their income than high earners
C  all earners pay the same amount
D  high earners pay a larger amount at a smaller share
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 A, 3 A, 4 B, 5 B, 6 A, 7 B, 8 A.
1. B names material well-being (A defines GDP, C confuses living standards with tax revenue, D confuses them with employment).
2. A divides the total by the population (B multiplies, C subtracts an unrelated item, D divides by workers, which gives output per worker rather than per head).
3. A divides correctly: N$40 billion / 2 million = N$20 000 (B multiplies instead of dividing, C drops a zero, D divides by 5 million).
4. B names health and access indicators (A is the money measure itself, C is an input to GDP per head, D is a trade figure rather than a living-standard indicator).
5. B names the averaging problem (A narrows GDP to one sector, C states a mechanical relationship that need not hold, D names a trade price rather than the distribution problem).
6. A names the sharing among households (B confuses it with the government budget, C names the average rather than the sharing, D names a single household's tax).
7. B links even sharing to a better typical household (A counts people rather than sharing, C names a money figure that says nothing about households, D names a flat tax without its effect on sharing).
8. A names the larger share from high earners (B describes a regressive income tax, C confuses the amount with the share, D describes a case that is regressive despite the larger amount).
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question, eight in total; the correct option is listed and each distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.
Each distractor traces to a named error: living standards confused with GDP, division misapplied, the average confused with the sharing, and a progressive tax confused with a regressive one.

items.prompt:
A report in the Etosha Observer, 2026: "The //Kharas region has grown fast since a new port project opened at the coast. Council figures show output per person well up, though the mayor of a settlement two hours inland notes that most of the new jobs and the piped-water points sit within 40 km of the port."

Table 1 - //Kharas region, 2021 and 2025
  GDP, 2021: N$12.0 billion
  GDP, 2025: N$16.8 billion
  population, 2021: 110 000
  population, 2025: 120 000
  share of households with piped water, 2021: 52%
  share of households with piped water, 2025: 61%
  mean years of schooling of adults, 2021: 8.1 years
  mean years of schooling of adults, 2025: 8.4 years
  life expectancy, 2021: 61 years
  life expectancy, 2025: 62 years

(a) Calculate GDP per head in 2025. [1]
(b) State the share of households with piped water in 2021. [1]
(c) Identify from Table 1 the change in life expectancy between 2021 and 2025. [2]
(d) Explain why GDP per head alone may mislead as a measure of living standards in this region. [4]
(e) Analyse what the data suggests about the change in living standards in the region between 2021 and 2025. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) GDP per head 2025 = N$16.8 billion / 120 000 = N$140 000 per person a year (N$16 800 million / 0.12 million people).
(b) 52% of households (from Table 1).
(c) Life expectancy rose from 61 years to 62 years, a rise of 1 year (from Table 1).
(d) GDP per head is an average, so it may hide how income is shared: in this region the mayor's note suggests the new jobs and water points cluster near the port, so the average of N$140 000 may stand over households two hours inland whose income and access moved far less. Because output may include goods that change household living standards little - project spending that passes through the region without reaching homes - the money figure may rise faster than the life people lead. Therefore the health, education and access indicators must be read alongside it, and they move differently: schooling crept up 0.3 years and life expectancy 1 year, both far behind the rise of about 28% in GDP per head (N$140 000 against about N$109 000), so the data itself warns that the money figure alone would flatter the change in living standards.
(e) As output per person rises, the indicators of living standards tend to rise with it over time - health, schooling and access to services travel in company with GDP per head. Here GDP rose from N$12.0 billion to N$16.8 billion, GDP per head from about N$109 000 (N$12.0 billion / 110 000) to N$140 000, piped water from 52% to 61%, schooling from 8.1 to 8.4 years, life expectancy from 61 to 62 years. Because GDP per head rose by about 28% while the service and health indicators rose by a few points or a single year, the growth in average output has not yet translated into matching gains for households - consistent with the clustering the mayor describes, since jobs and water points within 40 km of the port leave inland households outside much of the gain. Where the sharing of the new income is uneven - the extract suggests it is - the typical household's living standards lag the regional average, so the distribution of income, not the average, decides how most people live. However, four years may be too short for schooling and life expectancy to respond, since these indicators move slowly even where the gains are shared, and part of the population rise from 110 000 to 120 000 may be newcomers drawn to the port, which would hold the averages down while local living standards rose faster than the table shows. Port-side households gain jobs and water first, inland households gain least, children gain modestly in schooling, and the regional government gains revenue to extend services.
marking_guidance: Context: parts (a), (b) and (c) are read or calculated from the data; (d) and (e) must use the figures - the N$12.0 billion to N$16.8 billion GDP, the 110 000 to 120 000 population, the 52% to 61% water share, the 8.1 to 8.4 schooling years, the 61 to 62 life expectancy.
Reasoning: one mark per distinct linked statement; quoting a figure on its own is description, not analysis - the relationship must be stated and the reason given.
Conclusion: part (e) must run expected relationship, then evidence, then analysis, then an exception, and name for whom the effects land.
Refusal: an answer that lists figures without linking them earns at most the evidence marks, since figure-quoting is refused as analysis.

facts: GDP rose from N$12.0 billion to N$16.8 billion between 2021 and 2025
share of households with piped water rose from 52% to 61%
mean years of schooling rose from 8.1 to 8.4 years
life expectancy rose from 61 to 62 years

items.prompt:
A neighbouring country and Namibia are being compared for a school project on how people live.
(a) Define GDP per head. [2]
(b) Explain why health, education and access indicators are read alongside GDP per head when measuring living standards. [4]
(c) Analyse how the distribution of income is likely to affect the comparison of living standards between two countries with the same GDP per head. [6]
(d) Discuss whether a rise in a country's GDP per head means a rise in living standards for its people. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) GDP per head is the total value of the goods and services produced in a country in a given period - GDP - divided by the population, so it shows the average output available per person; it is the money figure used first when comparing living standards between countries or over time.
(b) GDP per head is an average, so it may hide how income is shared: where income is spread unevenly, the typical household may earn well below the average, and output may include goods that change living standards little. Because health, education and access indicators - life expectancy, mean years of schooling, clean water, electricity - measure outcomes households actually experience, they capture what the money figure may miss. Where two districts or countries post the same GDP per head yet differ on water, electricity and life expectancy, the wider indicators explain why the averages match while the lives do not. Therefore the honest measurement of living standards reads the indicators together with the money figure, since each may move differently in the short run.
(c) Suppose two countries record the same GDP per head - say N$60 000 a year - while the typical household in one earns about 70% of the average and in the other about 40%. Because the typical household's income pays for housing, schooling and healthcare, this causes the living standards the average household can afford to diverge: about 0.70 x N$60 000 = N$42 000 a year in the evenly shared country against about 0.40 x N$60 000 = N$24 000 a year in the unevenly shared one. The tax system may widen or narrow the gap further, since a progressive income tax takes a larger share from high earners and tends to narrow it while a regressive one takes a larger share from low earners and tends to widen it. Therefore a comparison that stops at GDP per head ranks the countries equal, while the typical household in one lives materially better - the sharing of income, not the average, decides the comparison. The typical household in the evenly shared country gains the more secure living standard, low-income households there sit closer to the average, and the government of the unevenly shared country faces a larger need for transfers and services to carry its worst-off households toward the average.
(d) Why it might: GDP per head is the average output available per person, so where the rise is broadly shared it tends to mean more food, housing, schooling and healthcare for households - and over time the health, education and access indicators tend to rise with it, which is the substance of living standards. Why it might not: because GDP per head is an average, the rise may be taken by a small group of households while the typical household's income barely moves; output may include goods that change living standards little; and where prices rise alongside output, a money gain may buy no more than before. Judgement: a rise in GDP per head is evidence that living standards may rise, not proof that they have - it depends on where the gain lands: provided the additional income is spread across households rather than clustered among a few, and provided prices do not eat it, the rise carries through to how people live; where the sharing is narrow or prices rise fast, the same headline rise leaves the typical household little better off, so the indicator to trust is the set - GDP per head read alongside health, education, access and the distribution of income - not the money figure alone.
marking_guidance: Parts (a) to (d) carry a model answer each; (d) is level-marked over three bands.
Context: (c) must use the figures given - the shared N$60 000 average and the 70% and 40% typical shares.
Reasoning: (c) one mark per distinct linked statement, tracing the chain from the sharing of income to the comparison of living standards.

Conclusion: (d) the top band examines why the rise might mean better living standards and why it might not, reaches a judgement, and names the condition the judgement depends on - where the gain lands and what happens to prices. Level 3 names both sides, judges and conditions it; Level 2 develops one side with a judgement; Level 1 makes points on one side without linking them.

facts: GDP per head is GDP divided by the population
the typical household may earn well below the average where income is spread unevenly
a progressive income tax takes a larger share from high earners; a regressive one takes a larger share from low earners

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "Discuss whether GDP per head is the best measure of a country's living standards." Build the plan from the measures and what each captures. Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for (the average that opens the comparison):
Chain 1: GDP per head divides the country's total output by its population -> the average available per person is shown, so countries of different sizes can be compared on the same scale -> it correlates over time with the goods households buy, so it is the natural first measure of living standards (for whom: households gain a single comparable figure; governments and firms gain a scale for planning).
Chain 2: GDP per head is one number collected consistently -> comparisons across countries and years are cheap and repeatable -> where it moves, something real about output per person has moved (for whom: examiners, statisticians and ministries gain a workable headline figure).
Case against (what the average may miss):
Chain 3: GDP per head is an average -> where income is spread unevenly, the typical household may earn well below it -> living standards for most people lag the headline -> the distribution of income, not the average, decides how the typical household lives (for whom: low-income households disappear inside the average; a rising headline may hide households whose living standards did not move).
Chain 4: output may include goods that change living standards little -> the money figure may rise without touching households' health, schooling or services -> health, education and access indicators - life expectancy, mean years of schooling, clean water, electricity - capture outcomes the money figure cannot -> two countries with equal GDP per head may keep different living standards (for whom: households gain the measures that track their lives; policy gains the indicators that locate need).
Judgement: GDP per head is the best single measure - no other one number scales output per person across countries and years - but it is not the best measure of living standards on its own: the honest measure is the set, GDP per head read alongside the distribution of income and the health, education and access indicators. The condition the judgement depends on is how income is shared and how far the money figure is eaten by prices: where the sharing is even and prices steady, GDP per head tracks how people live closely; where a small group takes the gain or prices rise fast, the same headline rise leaves the typical household little better off, and the wider indicators speak louder than the average.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the chains and the stated judgement are what is assessed.
Criterion: the decisive factor is where the gain lands - the sharing of income - and what the indicators say that the average cannot.
Counterargument: the case against must appear - the averaging problem, the distribution of income, and the outcomes the wider indicators capture.
Condition: the plan must end on what would change the judgement - the sharing of income and the movement of prices.
For whom: each chain names who gains and who loses - households, low-income households, governments, firms and statisticians.
